title: The Retail Silence That Reshapes The Amazon Stock Bull Case
detail:
The Retail Silence That Reshapes The Amazon Stock Bull Case
Trefis Team

Photo by justynafaliszek on Pixabay

Management's narrative has pivoted hard from optimizing its massive retail machine to funding aggressive AI infrastructure buildouts, quietly changing what an investment in the company is actually a bet on.

For the better part of two years, if you held Amazon (AMZN) stock, you were betting on efficiency. The story management told was about shaving pennies and seconds off the cost of moving a box from a warehouse to your door. Now, that efficiency story shares the stage with a much larger narrative. In its place is a focused narrative backed by hard numbers: management's plan to invest approximately $200 billion in cash capital expenditures in 2026, with the vast majority allocated to support AWS and AI infrastructure. The relative shift in focus matters, because it signals a profound shift in where Amazon's weight now sits, and what you, as a holder, are truly betting on today.

Fulfillment Efficiency Meets the AI Capital Wave

Not long ago, the company's earnings calls positioned retail logistics as the primary headline act. Management consistently highlights how they continue to lower per-unit fulfillment costs—with CFO Brian Olsavsky dedicating prepared remarks to regional inventory placement, consolidation rates, and scaling robotics. Optimizing North America retail remains a foundational engine, generating $426.3 billion annually (59% of revenue).

However, while cost-to-serve improvements remain steady in the background, the headline narrative and capital expenditure focus have decisively expanded toward Amazon Web Services (AWS) and AI infrastructure.

The New $169 Billion Story

The airtime has been seized by Amazon Web Services (AWS) and its all-in bet on artificial intelligence. The new story is one of staggering scale and acceleration. Management now leads with the fact that AWS is a "$169 billion annualized revenue run rate business." They are building a narrative around their custom silicon, now a business with a chips revenue run rate "over $25 billion," and an AI-specific revenue run rate also "over $25 billion." The center of gravity has moved decisively. While the North America retail segment posted steady full-year growth of 10% in FY2025, AWS grew 20% over the same period. That momentum carried directly into 2026, with AWS accelerating for its fifth consecutive quarter to deliver 37% year-over-year revenue growth in Q2. That is where the energy, the capital, and the story now live.

Why the Story Simply Moved On

This shift is reassuring. The moderated emphasis on retail efficiency doesn't appear to be hiding a problem; that segment is still a massive, profitable engine growing at 10%. Instead, the quiet reflects a deliberate choice to focus on a much larger, faster-growing opportunity. More than just another division, AWS's growth is now the primary driver of the entire company's valuation narrative.

title: The Price of Progress for Google Stock
detail:
The Price of Progress for Google Stock
Trefis Team
Tue, August 25, 2026 at 9:44 AM MDT 4 min read

MSFT
META
NFLX

Photo by ArcNovaStudio on Pixabay

If you hold Alphabet (GOOGL) stock, the recent top-line numbers look spectacular. In the second quarter of 2026, the company delivered 24% overall revenue growth, propelled by an 82% surge in its Google Cloud segment. This is the AI-fueled future investors have been waiting for. But beneath the surface of that growth, a fundamental shift is underway in the company's financial DNA, and it represents the most significant risk to the stock today.

The core issue is that the cost of competing in the AI arms race is so immense it's beginning to strain the famously efficient Alphabet financial model. This isn't a story about AI failing; it's a story about the price of ensuring it succeeds.

The AI Arms Race Is Draining the Coffers

"For years, Alphabet has been a reliable cash engine, generating $53.3 billion in free cash flow over the trailing twelve months. However, that run hit an unprecedented speed bump in the second quarter, when massive AI infrastructure spending pushed quarterly free cash flow into negative territory at -$5.9 billion. Management has raised its CapEx guidance to a range of $195 billion to $205 billion. Executives were clear that investors should expect that "free cash flow will remain under pressure."

The mechanism here is straightforward: spending on the technical infrastructure for AI, servers, data centers, networking, is consuming cash faster than the business generates it. This spending is seen as non-negotiable. As one analyst noted, there are concerns Google needs to keep pace with "other leading labs," and management itself stated that it "will need Gemini 4 as a larger base model to compete at that frontier level." If this investment doesn't produce a clear lead in AI, or if the returns prove elusive, investors could begin to question the entire strategy, which would pressure the stock's valuation multiple.

Profit Margins Are Sitting at a Five-Year Peak

Compounding the cash drain is the fact that Alphabet's profitability is currently at a cyclical high, giving it more room to fall than to rise. While Alphabet's headline net margin sits at an anomalous 55%—heavily inflated by non-operating unrealized gains on its equity investments—its core operating margin of 33% is genuinely at the high end of its multi-year range, well above its 3-year average of 31%.

These peak margins are now facing direct pressure from the AI investment cycle. The surge in CapEx leads to higher depreciation costs, which hits the operating margin line directly. Furthermore, management has signaled it will use more expensive third-party capacity to meet demand, warning this "will create modest margin pressure in the near term." A reversion of these historically high margins back toward their long-term average would significantly slow earnings growth, even if revenue continues to climb. At stake is the exceptional profitability that has long justified a premium for the stock.

title: The Real Question Behind Palantir Stock's High Price

The Real Question Behind Palantir Stock's High Price

Photo by ArtsyBee on Pixabay

The software firm looks expensive today, but the real debate is whether its rapid growth can deliver on the valuation discount that patience affords.

At a glance, Palantir Technologies (PLTR) stock looks expensive. Trading at about 115.6 times its last twelve months of adjusted earnings, it carries a premium that gives many investors pause. But that headline number is not the full story. For a patient holder, the price you are really paying on the earnings analysts expect two years from now is substantially lower.

On the consensus earnings forecast for 2027, today's share price of $175.89 works out to a multiple of about 87.4 times. That is a 24% discount from the trailing multiple, a gap that emerges as projected earnings grow into the current price. It is worth noting that while both multiples are on an adjusted basis, the definitions are not identical, so the compression reflects both powerful earnings growth and a slight shift in the earnings basis.

Is the Growth Behind the Discount Believable?

The honest question is not the price tag, but whether the growth that produces this discount will actually arrive. Analysts expect consensus revenue to grow about 58% a year through 2027. That might seem ambitious, but it is actually below what Palantir has been delivering. The company's revenue grew 79% over the last twelve months and accelerated to 93% in the most recent quarter.

Management's own outlook adds another layer of credibility. The company raised its full-year 2026 guidance for U.S. commercial revenue growth to about 134%. This segment is the engine, driven by what management on its latest call describes as immense demand from enterprises for "AI sovereignty," or the ability to retain full control over their own data and models. This rapid U.S. growth underpins the entire forecast. For more on where this growth is concentrated, it is worth noting that Palantir's sovereign AI boom is almost entirely in America. Still, the discount is provisional, not precise; the 20 analysts covering the stock are far apart on their 2027 earnings estimates, with a wide range from $1.61 to $2.94 per share.

And Palantir Technologies is far from alone: which 10 S&P 500 stocks carry the biggest hidden forward discount? Our rankings sort the entire index by how little you are really paying for each name's growth once the out-year earnings land.

The Margin of Safety and the Reward

A stock priced for this kind of growth can be volatile. In past market shocks, Palantir has fallen as much as 64% from its peak. The forward valuation discount, then, is best seen as a margin of safety, not a guaranteed gain.

title: 2 Tech Stocks I'd Load Up on Today and 1 I'd Avoid Until Further Notice

2 Tech Stocks I'd Load Up on Today and 1 I'd Avoid Until Further Notice

Over the past decade, tech stocks have been the go-to for many investors because of their performance and growth potential. The S&P 500's tech sector is up 771% in the past decade (as of Aug. 21), outperforming every other sector by a decent margin.

Many investors have tech exposure through major indexes like the S&P 500, Nasdaq Composite, or Dow Jones, but if you're looking for two individual tech stocks to add to your portfolio, Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZN) and Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) are two I would load up on. Tesla (NASDAQ: TSLA), however, is one I'd avoid. Let's take a look at the case for each.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Image source: The Motley Fool.
Don't underestimate the importance of diversification

One thing Amazon and Microsoft have in common, and why I'm high on both companies for the long term, is their diversified businesses. Amazon is a household name because of its e-commerce business, but it's far from its only work. It has cloud provider Amazon Web Services (AWS), Prime Video, advertising, Whole Foods, and even a pharmacy arm.

Microsoft is known for its Office software (Excel, Word, Teams, Outlook, etc.), but it also has its own cloud platform (Azure), its Windows operating system, hardware, Xbox, LinkedIn, advertising, and GitHub.

Having a foundational business -- Amazon with e-commerce and Microsoft with software -- is important for reliable cash flow and brand recognition, no doubt. However, multiple businesses and revenue streams can help sustain growth, even when a particular economic cycle isn't in your favor.

Cloud's importance will only increase

Both Amazon and Microsoft are known for other businesses, but there's a strong case that cloud computing is the most important business for both companies. AWS and Azure are the world's two largest cloud platforms, with market shares of 28% and 21%, respectively, as of the end of the first quarter.

Although e-commerce accounted for 79% of Amazon's $200.6 billion in revenue in the second quarter, AWS accounted for 61% of its operating income (profit from its core operations) while accounting for only 21% of its revenue. E-commerce generates the revenue needed to fund investments and expansion; AWS generates the profits.

Cloud remains Microsoft's main growth driver. In its most recent quarter, Microsoft's "Intelligent Cloud" segment (which includes Azure) brought in $39.3 billion in revenue, up 32% year over year. In Microsoft's latest fiscal year (ended June 30), Azure achieved its first $100 billion year, and the Microsoft Cloud segment as a whole brought in $214 billion. For perspective, Meta Platforms as a whole has generated just over $228 billion over its past four quarters.

I keep hitting the buy button on Salesforce (NYSE:CRM) because the agentic AI thesis I bought into is now showing up in the financials, and the market is finally starting to notice. Shares are up 27.74% over the past month and 9.47% in the past week, but the stock is still down 20.67% year to date from a start price of $263.53. That gap between what the business is doing and what the stock reflects is exactly why my cost basis keeps working lower.

AndreyPopov / iStock via Getty Images
What Keeps Pulling Me Back to the Buy Button

My thesis is simple: AI capital is rotating out of pure infrastructure and into the application layer where enterprise workflows actually live, and Salesforce owns that layer. Q1 FY27 (reported May 27, 2026) is the receipt. Revenue landed at $11.133 billion, up 13.27% year over year, and EPS came in at $3.88 against a $3.1271 consensus. That is the fifth consecutive quarter exceeding EPS expectations. Marc Benioff put it plainly: "Agentic AI is the biggest growth opportunity for our customers, and for Salesforce."

Three Reasons the Conviction Holds

First, the AI numbers are moving from slideware to actual ARR. Agentforce ARR reached $1.2 billion, up 205% year over year, and combined Agentforce plus Data 360 ARR reached nearly $3.4 billion. More than 50% of those bookings came from existing customers expanding commitments, which tells me the land-and-expand motion is intact.

Second, cash generation is doing the heavy lifting. FY26 free cash flow hit $14.402 billion, up 15.83%. That funded a $25 billion accelerated share repurchase, retiring 103 million shares, or roughly 11% of shares outstanding. There is a new $50 billion authorization behind it. Meanwhile, the dividend was raised to $0.44 per share.

Third, the valuation. CRM trades at a P/E of 24x with a forward P/E of 15x and an FCF yield of 8.41%. Total RPO of $72.4 billion, up 14%, gives me multi-year visibility.

Why CRM and Not the Usual Alternatives

The obvious reaches are Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT), ServiceNow (NYSE:NOW), and Oracle (NYSE:ORCL). Microsoft has broader AI exposure but trades at a much richer valuation than CRM's 15x forward multiple. ServiceNow is a fine business, but its multiple is also richer and its dividend is thinner. Oracle sells cloud infrastructure, which is what capital is rotating away from. Salesforce is the pure-play on agentic workflows, and analyst targets sit at $243.98 against today's $209.06.

Four stocks account for roughly 44.6% of Vanguard Growth Index Fund Admiral Shares (VIGAX). If you own this fund, you own a concentrated bet on NVIDIA, Apple, Alphabet, and Microsoft, wrapped in an index label. That is the story worth understanding before another dollar goes in.

Andrew Angelov / Shutterstock.com

VIGAX is the Admiral share class of Vanguard's large-cap growth index fund, tracking the CRSP US Large Cap Growth Index. It is a passive mutual fund with an ETF twin, VUG, and an Investor share class, VIGRX. Because Admiral, Investor, and ETF shares hold the same portfolio, holdings and performance below are drawn from Vanguard's most recent VUG fact sheet dated June 5, 2026, and VUG's live price history as of August 24, 2026.

A Growth Index That Is Really a Mega-Cap Tech Fund

The index label understates how top-heavy this portfolio has become. As of June 5, 2026, NVIDIA (NASDAQ:NVDA) sat at 13.3% of assets, Apple (NASDAQ:AAPL) at 12.3%, Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOGL) at 9.9%, and Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) at 9.1%. Round out the top 10 with Amazon (4.6%), Broadcom (4.4%), Meta (4.1%), Tesla (3.5%), Eli Lilly (2.6%), and Visa (1.7%), and a supposedly diversified index fund becomes something closer to a semiconductor-plus-platforms basket with a healthcare and payments sleeve attached.

On a $100,000 balance, roughly $65,000 is riding on the ten names above. That is the tradeoff investors accept in exchange for owning the growth style at index cost.

Act now: the analyst who called NVIDIA in 2010 just named his top 10 AI stocks — and VIGAX didn't make the cut. Grab the names FREE today.

Cheap, but the ETF Twin Is Cheaper

VIGAX's Admiral shares carry Vanguard's usual $3,000 minimum investment and an expense ratio in single basis points, keeping fee drag near the floor for retail funds. The ETF twin, Vanguard Growth ETF (NYSEARCA:VUG), lists a net expense ratio of 0.03% on its June 5, 2026 fact sheet, and it holds an identical portfolio with no minimum beyond one share. For investors in taxable accounts, the ETF wrapper also tends to distribute fewer capital gains than the mutual fund format. That is a meaningful reason to check whether VUG fits before defaulting to VIGAX.
